title: The Keeper of the Last Question
summary: Deep beneath the mountain sleeps a question so powerful that answering it would remake the world — or unmake it. Tamsin inherits the task of guarding it, and a lifetime of resisting the urge to know, and must decide whether some things are better left unanswered, and what it costs to guard a door you long to open.

chapters.title: The Question Beneath the Mountain
chapters.body:
Beneath the oldest mountain in the world, at the bottom of a stair that went down farther than any other stair, there was a small stone room, and in that room there was a question.

Not a person asking a question. The question itself — carved into the far wall in letters that seemed to shift when you weren't looking directly at them, glowing faintly with a light that was not quite any color. It was the Last Question: the deepest question there is, the one that lies underneath all other questions, the one that — if ever answered — would remake the whole world, or unmake it. No one knew which. That was rather the point. The question was so fundamental, so total, that to answer it would be to reach down to the very root of everything and pull — and whether that pull would remake reality into something greater, or simply unravel it into nothing, no one could say, because no one had ever dared to answer it.

And so, for as long as the mountain had stood, there had been a Keeper. One person, whose whole task was to sit in the small stone room at the bottom of the deepest stair, and guard the Last Question — which meant, above all, to not answer it. To resist, for a whole lifetime, the almost unbearable urge to speak the answer that would rise, unbidden, in the mind of anyone who sat long enough before those shifting glowing letters. Because the terrible thing about the Last Question was that it wanted to be answered. It pulled at the mind of whoever guarded it, offering up the answer, tempting them to speak it — to finally know, to finally see what would happen, to end the long unbearable not-knowing. And the Keeper's task, day after day, year after year, was simply to sit with that pull and never give in.

Tamsin was seventeen, and when the old Keeper died — died at last of great age, having guarded the question faithfully for sixty years and never once spoken the answer — the task passed to her. She descended the deepest stair, and entered the small stone room, and sat down before the Last Question for the first time, and felt, immediately, what every Keeper felt: the pull. The question glowing on the wall, shifting, reaching into her mind, offering up its answer, whispering wouldn't you like to know? Wouldn't you like to finally see? Just say it. Just answer. End the wondering. Know.

And Tamsin understood, with a sinking heart, what she had been given: a lifetime of sitting before the most tempting thing in the world, and never, ever giving in to it.

The old Keeper had left her a single written note, the only instruction. It said: The question will offer you its answer every day of your life. It will tell you that answering is brave, that knowing is good, that the not-knowing is unbearable and pointless. It will be very convincing. Guard the question anyway. Not because knowing is always wrong — but because some things, once answered, can never be un-answered, and some doors, once opened, can never be closed. Your task is not to answer. Your task is to protect the world from an answer it cannot take back. — The Keeper before you, and all the Keepers before her.

chapters.title: The Pull of Knowing
chapters.body:
The years passed, and Tamsin guarded the Last Question, and every single day it tried to make her answer it.

The pull never lessened. If anything, it grew more sophisticated. In her first years, the question tempted her simply — just say the answer, just know. But as Tamsin grew older and wiser, the question grew cleverer in its temptation, and began to reason with her, in her own voice, with her own best arguments.

Isn't knowledge good? it would whisper. Aren't you a seeker of truth? Every other question in the world, we answer — we praise the answering of questions, we call it wisdom, we call it courage, we call it progress. Why is this one question different? Why should this one truth stay hidden? Isn't hiding from a question just cowardice dressed up as duty? Think what you might learn. Think what the world might become. You've sat here for years resisting — but what if resisting is the mistake? What if the brave thing, the wise thing, the right thing, is finally to answer, and see, and know?

And these were hard arguments, because they were partly true. Tamsin did believe knowledge was good. She did believe questions were meant to be answered, that seeking truth was noble, that hiding from hard questions was usually cowardice. Everything in her education, everything in her nature, said answer the question. That's what you do with questions. You answer them. And the Last Question used all of that against her, every day, reasoning in her own voice that guarding it was cowardice and answering it would be brave.

There were days Tamsin nearly gave in. Days when the not-knowing felt truly unbearable, when the question's arguments seemed irrefutable, when she thought: what if I'm wasting my whole life guarding a door that should be opened? What if the Keepers before me were just frightened, and the real courage is to answer? She would sit before the shifting glowing letters with the answer rising in her throat, so close, so tempting, and it would take everything she had not to speak it.

But each time she came to the edge of answering, Tamsin made herself remember the one thing the question could never argue away. Some things, once answered, can never be un-answered. Some doors, once opened, can never be closed. The Last Question wasn't like other questions, and here was the difference the question always tried to make her forget: answering an ordinary question adds knowledge to the world, and if the knowledge turns out to be harmful, you can at least try to contain it, undo it, learn from the mistake. But the Last Question would remake or unmake the whole world in the instant it was answered — totally, permanently, irreversibly. There would be no containing it, no undoing it, no learning from the mistake, because there might be no world left to learn in, or a world so utterly changed that the old one was gone forever. And you do not gamble the entire world, permanently, on a bet you can never take back — no matter how noble the curiosity, no matter how convincing the argument, no matter how unbearable the not-knowing.

That was the thing the question could never defeat. Not because knowledge is bad. But because some answers cost more than any knowledge is worth, and some doors guard the world itself, and the wisdom to leave them closed — even when everything in you longs to open them — is the rarest and hardest wisdom there is.

chapters.title: The Door Left Closed
chapters.body:
Tamsin guarded the Last Question for sixty years, as the Keeper before her had, and never once spoke the answer — and the guarding did not get easier, and she never stopped longing to know. But near the end of her life, something happened that tested her as the daily pull never had.

A young seeker came down the deepest stair — a brilliant, passionate young scholar who had learned of the Last Question and had come, burning with conviction, to argue that it should be answered. And the young scholar made, out loud, every argument the question had been whispering to Tamsin for sixty years, and made them well. "You've wasted your life on cowardice!" the young scholar cried. "Hiding from the greatest truth there is! Knowledge is good — you know it's good — and here you sit, guarding ignorance, denying the world the answer to its deepest question! What right do you have to keep this from everyone? Answer it! Or step aside and let me! The not-knowing is unbearable and pointless, and history will call you a coward for guarding a door that should be flung open!"

And Tamsin — old now, and wise, and having fought this exact battle within herself every day for sixty years — was perhaps the only person in the world who could answer the young scholar, because she had felt every ounce of that conviction herself and had learned what lay beneath it.

"I understand you," she said gently. "Better than you know. Everything you're saying, I've said to myself, every day, for sixty years. You think I guard this question because I don't feel the pull of it. The truth is the opposite: I've felt the pull of it more than you ever could, for longer than you've been alive, and I've had to earn the choice to leave it closed every single day. So believe me when I tell you what you haven't yet understood." She gestured at the shifting glowing letters. "You're right that knowledge is good. You're right that most questions should be answered, that seeking truth is noble, that hiding from hard questions is usually cowardice. I believe all of that too. But this question is different, and the difference is the only thing that matters: answering it cannot be undone. Every other question we answer, we can learn from — if the answer harms us, we can contain it, correct it, try again. This one remakes or unmakes the whole world, permanently, in an instant, with no way back. And you do not gamble everything, forever, on an answer you can never take back — not for any amount of knowledge, not for any nobility of curiosity, not to end any amount of not-knowing."

"But how can you bear it?" the young scholar demanded. "To never know?"

"That," said Tamsin, "is the whole of the task. And here is what I've learned, that you haven't yet. It is not cowardice to leave some doors closed. It takes far more courage to guard a door you long to open than to open it. Anyone can answer a question — that's easy, it's the easiest thing in the world, to give in to the pull of knowing. The hard thing, the truly brave and wise thing, is to sit before the most tempting question there is, longing with all your heart to know, and to choose — freely, every day, forever — not to answer it, because you understand what it would cost. The world is full of people brave enough to open doors. What it desperately needs, now and then, is someone wise enough to guard one. Not out of fear of knowledge. Out of love for the world that the answer would unmake."

And the young scholar fell silent, because there was something in the old Keeper's words — the hard-won weight of sixty years of resisting — that could not be argued away.

Tamsin looked at the young scholar for a long moment, and then she made a choice. "You came here burning to answer the question," she said. "That fire — that longing to know, that conviction that truth should never be hidden — it's a good fire. The world needs it, almost everywhere. But it needs, too, the rare wisdom to know the one place where it must not be indulged. I've guarded this question my whole life, and I'm near the end now, and there must be a Keeper after me. And I think — I think it should be you. Not because you don't long to answer it. Because you long to answer it so much, and because you're brilliant enough to have made every argument for answering it, and because now you've heard why it must not be answered, and understood. A door is only truly guarded by someone who longs to open it and chooses not to. A Keeper who felt no pull would be no Keeper at all. It's the longing, mastered, that makes the guarding mean something."

And the young scholar — humbled, changed, and beginning to understand — became the next Keeper of the Last Question. And Tamsin died not long after, having guarded the question faithfully for sixty years and never once spoken the answer, and having passed the task to someone who would understand, at last, why it must be guarded: not because knowing is wrong, but because some doors hold the whole world, and the wisdom to leave them closed — while longing, always, to open them — is the rarest courage there is.

The Last Question still glows on the far wall of the small stone room at the bottom of the deepest stair, shifting, reaching, offering its answer to whoever guards it. And there is still a Keeper, in every generation, who sits before it, and longs to know, and chooses not to answer — protecting the world from a truth it could never take back, guarding a door that must never be opened, and proving, every single day, that the bravest thing is not always to open the door and know. Sometimes the bravest thing, and the wisest, and the hardest, is to sit before the door you most long to open, and to leave it closed, out of love for everything that lies on this side of it.
